societies.name: Not All Robots — Robot-supported bubble families
societies.society: Human households dependent on assigned robot providers

scope.continuity: Original AWA comic, opening social arrangement
scope.period: 2056 bubble-city life before the catastrophic air-system failure
scope.population: Living humans in functioning robot-supported bubble households
exclusions: Robots as humans in the participation denominator
Intentional sabotage as a settled fact

societies.description:
In 2056, robots have replaced almost the entire human workforce and each family is assigned a robot provider. People live in enclosed cities whose essential systems are also managed by robots. This is implemented dependence, not merely a forecast of future automation. Guarantees receive only a weak favorable estimate because household assignment supplies ongoing support while leaving families exposed to their providers and fragile city life-support systems. The later oxygen catastrophe demonstrates how consequential that dependence can be.

Robot control of work and the cities places effective authority near the autonomous-machine end. That does not make every robot benevolent or every individual provider all-powerful. A high, broad nonworking estimate follows the explicit replacement of human work and the exception of hairdressers, allowing for useful care, artistic activity, organization and other unpaid contributions. It is not a literal claim that all humans are idle. The point covers living residents before the air-system disaster; dead residents are not counted as liberated workers, and the review’s uncertainty over sabotage remains unresolved.

guarantees.basis: The publisher explicitly establishes assigned robot support for every family; city life-support dependency makes its security uncertain.

control.basis: Robots control the main workforce and bubble-city infrastructure; human dependence does not establish effective human ownership.

nonworking.basis: Near-total replacement with hairdressers as an explicit exception supports .85 [.5,1], a noncanonical broad estimate allowing useful unpaid work.

evidence.claim: The publisher explicitly establishes assigned robot support for every family; city life-support dependency makes its security uncertain.
evidence.locator: Bounded named-society economic and story sections

uncertainties: Reference-led provisional assessment; source limitations and editorial uncertainty remain explicit.

societies.name: Judge Dredd — Mega-City One’s robot economy
societies.society: Robot production and welfare under the Justice Department

scope.continuity: Comic city background and its Mongoose tabletop adaptation
scope.period: Established police-state robot economy, outside a particular citywide catastrophe
scope.population: Living human residents of Mega-City One
exclusions: A particular movie’s economy without separate verification
Every historical unemployment figure as one contemporaneous census
Destroyed or dead citizens as leisure beneficiaries

societies.description:
Robots perform most ordinary production and services in Mega-City One, including skilled tasks as well as drudgery. Human employment becomes scarce and welfare supports a large dependent population. Material guarantees are rated weak rather than absent: benefits exist, but inadequate housing and official hostility to recipients make a secure universal floor doubtful. The estimate concerns the established system, not a moment when a catastrophe has destroyed ordinary provision.

The Justice Department concentrates political authority and governs the robot-supported city. Machines doing jobs do not automatically become the sovereign, so control remains near the concentrated human-elite position. The setting describes widespread boredom and abundant leisure, supporting a high but broad editorial nonworking estimate. Published unemployment numbers vary by period and measure formal employment, not all useful activity; none is copied directly as this axis. Care, art, study and informal work can continue. The verified comic and tabletop depictions are tagged, while film adaptations are left out until their economic arrangements are separately established.

guarantees.basis: Automatic production and substantial welfare coexist with inadequate housing and explicit official hostility toward welfare recipients.

control.basis: The human Justice Department retains concentrated authority; productive robots are not by themselves rulers.

nonworking.basis: Extensive leisure and displaced work support .8 [.45,.98] as an editorial direction; varying formal-unemployment figures are not a census of useful activity.

evidence.locator: Bounded named-society economic and story sections

review_notes: Twelve sequential decisions, two retained robot-supported human societies and one resolved duplicate program.
Not All Robots has an explicit human workforce-replacement premise; surviving hairdressers and useful unpaid activity qualify the nonworking estimate.
Mega-City One welfare and robot displacement are verified, but varying unemployment statistics are not copied into the participation axis.
Only comic and tabletop Mega-City One economies were verified; movie tags are not inherited automatically.
Metalzoic machine ecology, Harvester scale and robot rights alone do not establish an applicable human provision population.
No full comic runs, novels, sourcebooks or PDFs were retrieved; unrelated pinball and food-industry search matches were discarded.
